newsitem.title: FINLAND: Finland Bank sees stable monetary conditions in 97.
newsitem.headline: Finland Bank sees stable monetary conditions in 97.

text.p: The Bank of Finland said on Wednesday it expected cost and price developments to remain subdued with core inflation within the two percent target range and monetary conditions stable this year.

"The central bank estimates that cost and price developments will remain subdued in 1997 and that inflation will stay clearly within range of the approximate two percent target," it said in a statement summarising the leading article in its quarterly Markka & Talous review.
"Public finances will be further consolidated this year, and monetary conditions should remain stable," the Bank said.
"Stable interest rates are an essential requirement for balanced and sustainable growth," it said.

Confidence in the prospects for the Finnish economy had improved, but "the acceleration of economic growth and increase in asset prices have not been reflected in higher inflation or inflation expectations," the Bank of Finland said.
Consumer confidence in the future had been boosted by positive economic news and lower interest rates, the central bank said, adding private consumption had picked up.
Subdued inflation would help keep the markka stable amid growing uncertainty around EMU, the Bank of Finland said.
"Growing speculation concerning participants and timing of stage three of EMU has caused some tension within the ERM," it said.
"Moderate price developments and a further narrowing of Finland's public sector deficit will help to ensure continued stability in the value of the markka," it added.

Last year, Finland met the EMU convergence criteria on public sector debt, deficit, inflation and long-term interest rates, and "it is estimated that Finland will meet the convergence criteria again in 1997, by an even greater margin than last year," the central bank said.
But the deficit of central government finances was too high, it warned.

"Fulfilment of the criteria for stage three of EMU does not necessarily imply that public finances are in good shape," it said, calling last year's central governmernt deficit to GDP at 7.0 percent "unsustainably high in the long run."
"It is therefore important to take advantage of the economic boom to further consolidate central government finances," the Bank of Finland said.
